gist: In a solo episode, Nate Hagens argues that GDP growth is a biophysical anomaly funded by debt claims that have outrun the net energy surplus (the 'Wile E. Coyote gap'). He lays out seven ways growth ends, with 'biophysical musical chairs' as his main bet, and points to France's 10-year yield breaking 5%, US debt growth, a record-low SPR and the debt-funded, energy-constrained AI build-out as live warning signs.

insights.claim: Hagens argues that GDP is essentially a tally of energy and materials pulled through the economy, and that technology has never anywhere let the economy grow while physical throughput stayed flat.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: Growth forecasts that assume decoupling from resources are, in his view, unfounded.

insights.claim: Historically, materials use and GDP are correlated about one-for-one and energy about 0.7; 3% annual growth means GDP doubles about every 23 years, so in 70 years GDP would be 8x larger, requiring more than 4x the energy and about 800 billion tons of material a year versus today's 100.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: The 3% perpetual-growth assumption in government and pension plans conflicts with physical constraints.

insights.claim: Hagens says every government and pension fund assumes roughly 3% annual growth in perpetuity, which he believes the physical base cannot support.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: Long-dated liabilities priced on perpetual growth are at risk.

insights.claim: Money is the proximate driver of the economy and energy applied to materials is the ultimate driver; as the cheapest oil and richest ores were depleted, society 'printed more claims' against a shrinking surplus, which delayed the feedback from physical limits.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: Financial claims have outgrown the real resource base, so a reconciliation is coming.

insights.claim: Using his 'Wile E. Coyote' framing, Hagens says the Western economy has already run off the cliff, and financial markets will be what eventually makes society 'look down' en masse.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: He sees the trigger for the end of growth as financial.

insights.claim: Hagens says that since the great financial crisis almost all measured growth has been borrowed or government-driven, deficits have become permanent, and France's government spending is 57% of its economy.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: Growth increasingly depends on deficits and debt.

insights.claim: The US added more to its national debt in each of 2025 and 2026, both non-recession years, than in 2009, and the Strategic Petroleum Reserve is at its lowest level since it was first filled.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: Fiscal and physical buffers are both depleted heading into 2027.

insights.claim: The financial gap can close 'hot' through inflation and currency erosion or 'cold' through debt deflation like the 1930s, or through inflation first followed by a bond-market-triggered deflationary depression.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: Investors need hedges against both inflation and deflation.

insights.claim: Last week France's 10-year yield went above 5% for the first time in 25 years, spreads over Germany blew out, French credit-default swaps hit historic highs, Italian and Greek yields jumped in sympathy, and the euro hit a two-year low.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: Contagion in eurozone sovereign debt is the risk to watch.

insights.claim: Hagens says France is too big to save, and that forced spending cuts (a few percent off public spending and wages, frozen pensions) combined with an Iran-war fuel shock have put millions of people in the streets, with a city hall burned and thousands arrested.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: Even mild austerity can trigger severe political instability in overshoot economies.
insights.quote: France, specifically France, is too big to save.

insights.claim: Rising global bond yields are driven partly by the Israel-US-Iran war pushing up energy prices and central banks hiking in response, which exposes the weakest borrowers first.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: Energy shocks are being passed through into sovereign credit stress.

insights.claim: AI borrowing now competes with the US government for the same lenders, a handful of companies account for most expected S&P 500 earnings growth this quarter, and a growing share of the build-out is debt-funded and circular, with chipmakers funding their own customers.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: Debt-financed, concentrated AI capex is a systemic fragility for credit and equity markets.

insights.claim: The AI build-out is already short of power, transformers and copper, and lenders are starting to admit it is effectively a bet on cheap, abundant energy showing up.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: Energy and grid hardware are the binding constraint on AI returns.

insights.claim: Net investment has been stuck around 3% of GDP for over a decade and total factor productivity has not moved (slightly negative), which Hagens compares to gross versus net energy: gross GDP rises while net benefit does not.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: He doubts that AI has yet produced real productivity gains.

insights.claim: AI accelerates several of the seven risks: energy-hungry capital in risk one, job destabilization in risk three, surveillance in risk four and the speed of cyberattacks in risk seven; he also sees growing risk of a merger between big AI companies, government, surveillance and the military.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: AI raises tail risks rather than reliably offsetting them.

insights.claim: Hagens's main bet among the seven pathways is 'biophysical musical chairs': financial claims compound while the net energy surplus thins until there are not enough 'chairs' for every financial promise.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: He expects the end of growth to show up first as a financial crisis.

insights.claim: The other pathways are: a great-power or nuclear war breaking just-in-time trade; social unrest 'tearing it down from below'; authoritarian control by decree (Turkey's lira lost about 80% after Erdogan forced rates down); ecological limits under Liebig's Law of the Minimum; external shocks such as a Carrington-scale solar storm or an earthquake under Taiwan's fabs; and 'everything else'.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: This gives a checklist of tail risks for scenario planning.

insights.claim: Ecological limits are the one risk that becomes more certain the longer growth continues, as soils, aquifers, fisheries, pollinators and phosphorus mines are depleted and insurers pull out of entire regions.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: Insurance, agriculture and water stress will intensify over time.

insights.claim: Hagens says there are currently zero fertilizer exports coming out of Hormuz, an example of single-input supply-chain fragility.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: Fertilizer and food prices are exposed to the Gulf conflict.

insights.claim: By the 'law of aggregate probability', the odds that all seven risks are avoided year after year keep shrinking, so at least one triggering seems near-certain to him.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: Assuming continuity is itself a concentrated bet.

insights.claim: Past failed predictions (Malthus, Ehrlich, Limits to Growth) were rescued by real new surplus such as the carbon pulse, globalization, debt and central-bank backstopping since 2009, but none repealed the limits, and substitution cannot replace net energy, the 'master resource'.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: An energy transition itself requires a large upfront energy outlay drawn from a shrinking surplus.

insights.claim: Even a 50% drop from today's peak material wealth would leave the average human better off than anyone before our grandparents; Hagens advises reducing personal fragility and building real wealth (skills, community, soil, water) over financial claims.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: He argues for resilience-oriented personal positioning rather than nihilism.
